newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia journalist says Malaysia prison appalling.
newsitem.headline: Australia journalist says Malaysia prison appalling.

text.p: An Australian journalist detained in Malaysia along with organisers of a conference on human rights in East Timor said on Monday she had been kept in appalling conditions.
"Conditions in the prison holding cell were appalling," Catherine McGrath, Singapore-based correspondent for Australian Broadcasting Corp (ABC) radio, told the radio station.
She said 20 women were held in three cells.
"We asked repeatedly for fresh water -- there was no fresh water given," she said.

"I asked repeatedly for access to the Australian High Commission or a representative of the Australian High Commissioner and that was denied, and I was not allowed to see a lawyer either until the next day."

Malaysian police on Saturday arrested and detained 46 foreign activists attending the second Asia Pacific Conference on East Timor in Kuala Lumpur. Two foreign journalists were also detained, including McGrath.
Some of the activists were then deported including Australian Andrew McNaughtan, convenor of the Australia East Timor Association in the state of New South Wales.
McGrath was released on Sunday on her own recognisance.

Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer repeated on Monday the Australian government's position that although the incident was unfortunate, delegates were aware that the Malaysian government had banned the conference.
"The incident clearly is an unfortunate incident, but the fact is the organisers were clearly told that the conference was to be banned," Downer told ABC radio.
"The warning signs had been there and in those circumstances, the Malaysian government and authorities are entitled to enforce Malaysian law."

Asked if he was concerned about the treatment of Australians under detention, Downer said: "In the case of the vast majority of the Australians, they didn't suffer the conditions that Catherine McGrath suffered."
Downer had just heard McGrath's account from Singapore.
He added: "Those people were eventually put in a hotel at the airport and the last I heard was that four had been deported. Probably more have by now."
A Malaysian minister had warned early last week that the government did not want the conference to take place because it could harm bilateral ties with Indonesia, Downer said.
Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975 after the abrupt departure of its Portuguese colonisers and now rules the territory in defiance of the United Nations.
